title: SREcon26 Americas - From ESXi to Kubernetes: Modernizing 1,400 Edge Locations with Open Source
transcriptText:
Good afternoon everyone and thank you
for being here. I hope the coffee has
been kicked in and you are all excited
for this session. I'm Kaneka and
together with my colleague Jazjit, we
are here to share a story that I think a
lot of you will find familiar. It's a
story about inheriting stable system
hitting a wall and figuring it out how
to modernize it anyway under real scale
at real constraints. The talk is called
from exxi to kubernetes at edge
modernizing 1400 distributed locations
and I really want to emphasize on the
number 1400 because these are 1400
retail stores nationwide each one is a
light production environment
for those who may not be familiar with
us. Lobla is Canada's leading food and
pharmacy retailer. We serve millions of
Canadians every week through a network
of grocery stores,armacies,
and digital platforms that span across
the country. Lobla has over 2,800
locations generating a 61 billion
revenue. We're doing more than billion
customer transactions per year and we
are a healthcare partner to more than
20% of Canadians.
Our portfolio includes well-known brands
like Loblaws, No Frills, Joe, Shoppers,
Drug Mart, and PC Financial. Each
division playing a critical role in how
Canadians access their everyday
essentials. Joe is our clothing and
apperal line of business. PC Financial
is the banking institute and Shoppers
Drug Mart is the pharmacy business and
the core business for today's talk.
Shoppers Drug Mart is a network of
10,000 healthcare professionals caring
for 11 million Canadians. At the scale
we operate, reliability isn't just the
technical goal. It's directly tied to
how Canadians get their prescriptions
and the services that they depend upon
daily. And that's exactly where site
reliability engineering becomes
essential.
So what led to the transformation from
EXI to Kubernetes? We weren't trying to
modernize just for the sake of
modernization. The system we had was
very stable and was running on our
stores reliably for years. Each location
had its own small EXSI based environment
running critical pharmacy and point of
sale workloads across the country. That
meant roughly around 1,400 distributed
edge locations had their own EXSI
environment.
The first pressure came from the cost.
Virtualization licensing cost increased
significantly and the economics no
longer made sense at that scale. But
cost wasn't alone the only problem. The
existing platform was fundamentally
designed around virtual machines and
that made application modernization very
difficult. Running containers adopting
microservices were not a natural fit in
this environment.
So while the platform was stable for
today, it would have become increasingly
expensive for tomorrow and it
effectively limited our ability to
modernize. That's what ultimately pushed
us to explore a different approach. With
that context, I'll pass it to my
colleague JJ to take you through what we
did next.
>> Thank you Keka. That was a great
overview of the business and the problem
statement.
So for those I haven't met I'm just je
I'm part of the Loblast team and I have
worked on the edge modernization
initiative we are presenting today. I'll
take it up from here and walk you
through the journey ahead
to understand why this migration was
complex. It will help to understand what
a typical store looked like before we
even started.
Each store had a self-contained ESXi
environment, usually two physical nodes,
a shared storage and multiple virtual
machines running business critical
workloads.
And these stores had to operate even in
case of connectivity loss to a data
center or cloud.
The applications themselves were mostly
traditional enterprise workloads. Java
applications, DB2 and point of sale
systems all running inside VMs.
Monitoring was also very tightly coupled
to the platform. We were using a
proprietary tool from IBM called as IT
CAM. The current system was optimized
for stability but not flexibility.
Which is exactly why replacing it safely
was hard.
So it wasn't just a migration. It meant
changing the foundation of every store.
Before we talk about the solution, it's
important to understand the environment
we were operating in. Yes, we had some
hard constraints. We had no budget to go
and buy the best and the latest
hardware.
We never wanted to venture into another
proprietary software and our stores
being customerf facing had very less
tolerance to downtime.
To top it up, the pharmacy management
system we were using was a legacy Java
application built inhouse. Rewriting all
those into microservices was not
feasible in the migration timelines we
had. But the real challenge came with
the edge environment itself.
Each store had limited storage and
compute. network wasn't the best at
every store and there were no platform
engineers on site to fix things when
they broke.
Whatever we had to build had to be done
remotely and resilient by default.
All these constraints weren't
negotiable. They defined the operating
procedure for us and we had to design a
platform that works under these
constraints and that challenged every
decision we made.
The answer was simplification not
replacement.
Modernize without new hardware.
Eliminate proprietary
licensing. Standardize on opensource.
So we build on what we had.
We started with the base of open suza
and then we installed Kubernetes on top
of it and then we introduced cubeword.
So cube was our bridge to let us run
legacy VMs inside Kubernetes so that we
don't have to rewrite everything as
microservices.
At the end, every store became a small
declarative data center where every
component was open-source.
The goal wasn't Kubernetes here. The
goal was to make every store manageable
the same way.
But architecture is one thing. Replacing
a live platform is another.
To migrate our stores safely, we
designed a four-step process where every
step was reversible and roll back was
always possible.
The first step, the pre-cut over phase,
we introduced a third node into the
store. And mind this is not a new node
we bought. This was a node already
existing in the store whose workload had
been previously migrated to cloud. So we
repurposed that node to install a
Kubernetes cluster alongside the ESXi
environment.
Now this gave us a safe way to validate
Kubernetes workloads without even
touching the production system.
During this phase we also took the
opportunity to simplify architecture.
We decoupled components from the
pharmacy VM. We moved one pharmacy
component to a small dedicated VM that
was IBM messaging Q.
We were also able to modernize or
convert 10 pharmacy applications as
microservices.
So all this helped us to make the
pharmacy VM significantly lighter. So
from running a pharmacy VM with 32GB
memory, we came to a VM running 18 GB
memory. And all this was done to reduce
the tight dependencies which directly
aligns with the core S sur principles
around isolation and safer changes.
Second was the cut over night and that's
a showtime.
Cutovers were usually done after the
stores were closed. We consolidated the
workloads on one single ESXi node that
freed up another node and we expanded
the Kubernetes cluster to a two node
cluster.
data was then synced and IPs were
switched. But one important point to
note here is there's still one ESXi node
available which we kept intact with the
old VMs but in a shutdown state.
So this gave us a safe end state to the
night where now applications are running
on Kubernetes but we still have an ESXi
node in case there are issues and we
have to roll back.
We never replace the system in one step.
We replaced it in safe layers. The ESX
IIO here was our insurance policy.
Only after the stores confirmed
operations, the next day we would go
ahead and convert the ESXi node into
Kubernetes and make it a full three node
cluster. The diagram here shows the
final state of our stores.
The key idea was simple. Never make a
irreversible change until the new state
has proven itself under production load.
Now, how did we deploy and monitor these
systems?
Our deployment strategy was simple,
imperative to bootstrap, declarative at
a steady state. We used Enible to bring
up the OS and install Kubernetes. After
that everything was gitdriven.
The key design design decision here was
the hub and spoke githops model.
This allowed us to do control rollouts
across clusters without overloading git
or the network.
So instead of edge clusters polling git
every hour, we introduced a management
cluster which acted as a hub. The hub
pulls Git Ops repo, detects changes and
then performs a pushbased reconciliation
to our edge clusters. Note the git still
remains our source of truth but now
reconciliation is controlled and
centralized.
Observability being the core SR
principle was built in from day one. We
had Otal collectors collecting logs and
metrics, pushing data to purpose-built
backends like Loki, Click House,
Victoria Betrics. Graphana was used for
visualizing and alerting.
At last, the results were deterministic,
repeatable, and we had drift-free
deployments across stores.
Now, how did we scale to 1400?
What made this possible was a small team
but focused. We had a group of five
SRRES who were focusing on platform
automation and reliability.
A TPM managing the program and four
deployment specialists who were carrying
over the nightly cuts. The key wasn't
the team size here. It was having
repeatable automated processes.
We intentionally started slow migrating
one store a night to validate our
process and uncover any edge cases we
might have missed. After each
deployment, we used to refine our
runbooks, improve our automation and
strengthen our roll back procedures.
Once the process was predictable and and
repeatable, we scaled to around 10
stores per night and at max capacity we
were doing around 40 stores a week while
still maintaining operational safety.
The scaling factor here weren't more
ingenious. It was better automation and
safer runbooks.
The impacts of migration were
measurable. At last, we could eliminate
all licensing cost for OS virtualization
and monitoring across stores. We
standardize the platform across all
stores. Reliability improved because of
Kubernetes self-healing features. And
most importantly, the platform now
supports modernization without another
migration.
The economics and operations both got
better.
With that, I would want to leave you all
with the key takeaways and the lessons
we have learned. Applying S sur
principles, especially automation,
wasn't optional for us. It was a must
for such kind of migrations.
And what made this migration possible
were small but deliberate choices.
Standardizing the platform, going
declarative, using GitOps, and designing
every step to be reversible.
We kept asking ourselves two questions.
Can this be rebuilt deterministically?
Can this scale without people? And if
the answer was no, we would go back to
the drawing board.
The biggest lesson we learned is
modernization isn't about new tools.
It's about reducing operational surface
area.
The discipline of execution matters more
than the tech stack. And that is what
made this migration work.
Thank you everyone.
